options: Passes one of its data inputs through, chosen by a select input
Combines two inputs into one value
Routes one input to one of several outputs
Stores the selected value
drills.why: Routing one input to one of several outputs is its dual, the demultiplexer. Between them they are the two halves of every routing decision in a machine.

drills.q: What distinguishes a control wire from a data wire in the circuit?
options: Nothing. A control signal is an ordinary input into ordinary gates
Control wires carry a different voltage
Control wires connect to a special input on the gate
Control wires are evaluated before data wires
drills.why: There is no control input on a NAND gate. The only difference is what a human decided to call it, which is why "control is data" is the sentence to keep from this unit.

drills.q: Writing a multiplexer as "if sel then b else a" is:
options: True about what it computes and false about what it is, since both
Exactly right
Wrong, because a multiplexer cannot express a conditional
Right only when the inputs are constant
drills.why: All the gates are always powered and both partial results are always being computed. The select decides which answer reaches the output and the other is discarded at full cost.

drills.q: Why does that matter for a GPU twelve parts from here?
options: Computing both sides and discarding one is what logic does naturally, so
GPUs use multiplexers where CPUs use branches
It does not; the cases are unrelated
GPUs cannot express conditionals
drills.why: A processor that skips work has to be built specially to do it. Warp divergence is usually presented as surprising, and it is closer to what a circuit does if you leave it alone.

drills.q: An arithmetic unit with no control signal asserted is:
options: Still computing, on whatever its inputs happen to be
Idle and drawing no power
Holding its previous result
Undefined
drills.why: It is combinational. A control signal does not start it, it decides whether anyone reads the answer. "The ALU runs when you tell it to" is a misconception worth naming early.

drills.q: How many select bits does a multiplexer with 16 inputs need?
drills.why: 2^k inputs need k bits, and that relationship is where the word address comes from.

options: A position among things, not a name for one
A number stored in the cell it refers to
A label the machine looks up in a table
A pointer to a name
drills.why: Sixteen unnumbered streets with sixteen unnumbered houses: the fourth house on the seventh street still locates a house and no plaque is needed. Nothing in the circuit stores an address.

drills.q: Where do the address bits actually go?
options: Onto the select inputs of a tree of multiplexers and decoders
Into a lookup table of addresses
Into a comparator against every stored address
Into a register that indexes memory
drills.why: There is no table of addresses anywhere. There is a tree, and the address bits are the select signals on it.

drills.q: A decoder with k inputs raises how many of its outputs?
options: Exactly one of 2^k
All 2^k
k of them
It depends on the input pattern
drills.why: Exactly one, which is what makes it useful as a set of enables. It is a demultiplexer with its data input held at 1.

drills.q: Building a four-way multiplexer as a tree of two-way ones costs:
options: More stages of delay and fewer gates than building it flat
Fewer stages and fewer gates
More stages and more gates
The same either way
drills.why: It is the same gates-against-delay trade as everything in Part I. The tree scales better, which is why a memory of any real size is a tree rather than a flat decode.

drills.q: "Which register do I write to" is implemented by:
options: A demultiplexer on the write-enable signal
A comparator on the register number
A lookup table in the control unit
A dedicated register-select circuit
drills.why: And "which register do I read from" is a multiplexer on the outputs. Not parts like those. Those parts.

drills.q: A multiplexer whose inputs are "what is here" and "what is arriving" is:
options: A hold-or-load, which becomes a register once there is a clock
A comparator
Already a register
An adder
drills.why: It is not yet a register, because "what is here" means the output feeding back to the input, and that loop is illegal without a clock. The circuit is incomplete rather than wrong.

drills.q: Why is a register not simply a flip-flop with its output tied to its input?
options: There would be no way to ever load a new value into it
The loop would oscillate
Flip-flops cannot drive their own inputs
It would work, but use too much power
drills.why: nand2tetris labels that diagram "invalid design" for exactly this reason. The fix is a multiplexer in the loop, and the multiplexer's select bit is what load means.

drills.q: When the machine executes an instruction, what looks up its meaning?
options: Nothing. Bits of the instruction are wired to select inputs and route
A microcode interpreter
The instruction decoder, which holds a table of meanings
The assembler, at compile time
drills.why: NAND gates do not know what they are doing, and a million of them connected together still do not. That is the answer to the question in Scott's title.

drills.q: A design that ignores one of its inputs is:
options: Fine, and costs nothing
An error, because every input must be driven
Wasteful, because the input still consumes power
Only allowed at the top level
drills.why: Leaving an input unused is allowed; reading a wire that nothing drives is not, and those are different mistakes. Ignoring inputs is how one part serves several purposes on a shared bus.
